title: Modeling the Nonlinear Dynamics of Intracellular Signaling Networks
author: Oleksii S. Rukhlenko
license_note: PMC full-text XML — Bio-protocol — CC-BY confirmed in article XML

steps.title: Construct ODE network model
steps.instruction: Build an ODE model of the signaling network using the known interaction topology. Implement the model in a software package that can export SBML, such as COPASI or BioNetGen.

steps.title: Define kinetic expressions
steps.instruction: For interactions with known kinetics, model them mechanistically; for all other connections use hyperbolic multipliers α_ij = (1 + γ_ij·x_j / K_j) / (1 + x_j / K_j), where γ_ij > 1 indicates activation, γ_ij < 1 inhibition, and γ_ij = 1 no regulation (α_ij = 1). Set K_ij as the activation/inhibition constant. Specify parameter ranges using protein abundances and kinetic constants, assign numerical values, non‑dimensionalize the model to reduce the number of parameters, and export the finalized model to SBML format.

steps.title: Sample parameter space with DYVIPAC
steps.instruction: Import the SBML model into the DYVIPAC package, sample the parameter space, and determine the number and stability of steady states for each parameter set to identify observable dynamical regimes.

steps.title: Derive 2‑D reduced model
steps.instruction: Rank protein abundances in descending order, select the two most abundant proteins, and apply the quasi‑steady‑state (QSS) approximation for all other proteins to reduce the full ODE system to a two‑dimensional model.

steps.title: Analyze nullclines and validate dynamics
steps.instruction: Using the steady‑state specifications and the shapes of nullclines, determine the dynamic regimes of the 2‑D model and validate them by numerically integrating the ODEs (compute nullclines, vector fields, identify stable/unstable steady states and limit cycles).

steps.title: Repeat reduction for additional protein pairs
steps.instruction: If more than two proteins have high and comparable abundances, create a list of all such protein pairs and repeat the QSS reduction and subsequent analysis for each pair.

steps.title: Scan 2‑D parameter planes for bifurcations
steps.instruction: Systematically scan two‑parameter planes, identify bifurcation types (e.g., saddle‑node, Andronov‑Hopf), map borders separating distinct dynamic regimes, and predict previously unobserved regimes for later experimental validation.

steps.title: Identify limit‑cycle regimes
steps.instruction: Scan parameters to locate regimes containing foci and determine the appearance or annihilation of limit cycles.

steps.title: Fit model to time‑series data
steps.instruction: If time‑series data are available, fine‑tune model parameters to reproduce the observed trajectories using standard parameter‑optimization tools (e.g., packages cited by Glover et al., Maiwald & Timmer, Kreutz & Timmer, Penas et al., Thomas et al., Degasperi et al., Mitra et al.).

steps.title: Extend model to PDE with transport
steps.instruction: Add mass‑transfer terms describing diffusion and convection to the ODE system to derive a partial‑differential‑equation (PDE) model.

steps.title: Run spatiotemporal simulations
steps.instruction: Perform spatiotemporal simulations of the PDE model using software such as OpenFOAM, FiPy, or Virtual Cell.

steps.title: Access example scripts
steps.instruction: Download the “examples.zip” archive to obtain example Python scripts and data illustrating the analysis of the RhoA‑Rac1 signaling network model.
